title: Cellulitis and abscess: when to drain, when to cover MRSA

source.citation: Written for Blackout, 2026-09-13. Based on the IDSA skin and soft tissue infection guideline. Not tied to an article; review before trusting.

questions.q: Uncomplicated cellulitis with no pus and no systemic signs. Which antibiotic is appropriate?
questions.why: Nonpurulent cellulitis is nearly always streptococcal, so a beta-lactam is enough. MRSA cover is added only with pus, penetrating trauma, or a known MRSA history.

questions.q: What is the primary treatment of a simple skin abscess?
questions.why: Antibiotics are added when there are systemic signs, immunosuppression, multiple abscesses, or drainage has failed, and then they cover MRSA.

questions.q: Which oral antibiotics cover community-acquired MRSA?
questions.why: Clindamycin also covers streptococci but local resistance can be high. For purulent cellulitis, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole or doxycycline is the usual choice.

questions.q: How long is a course of antibiotics for uncomplicated cellulitis?
questions.why: Five days was as effective as ten in trials. Marking the border with a pen at the first visit makes the improvement, or its absence, obvious at 48 hours.

questions.q: Pain out of proportion to the findings, rapid spread, and crepitus. What is this until proven otherwise, and what is the key step?
d: An abscess; incision and drainage in clinic
questions.why: Antibiotics are broad and include clindamycin for toxin suppression, but surgery is what saves the patient. Imaging must not delay it.

questions.q: Both lower legs are red, warm and swollen in a patient with varicose veins. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: Cellulitis is almost never bilateral. Elevation, compression and a topical steroid treat stasis dermatitis, and antibiotics do nothing for it.

questions.q: A patient has had four episodes of leg cellulitis in a year. Which preventive measure is recommended?
questions.why: Also treat the doorway: tinea pedis, oedema, and venous insufficiency. Recurrence falls while prophylaxis continues and returns when it stops.

questions.q: Which antibiotic is used after a cat or dog bite?
questions.why: It covers Pasteurella, which cephalexin and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole do not. Prophylaxis is given for cat bites, hand bites, and immunocompromised patients.

questions.q: A diabetic foot ulcer has surrounding cellulitis and a probe reaches bone. What does that finding indicate?
questions.why: Diabetic foot infections are polymicrobial and get broader cover than simple cellulitis. Osteomyelitis needs imaging, often a bone biopsy, and weeks of therapy.

questions.q: Which features move cellulitis from oral to intravenous therapy?
a: Systemic signs such as fever and tachycardia
questions.why: Severe infection is treated with vancomycin plus a beta-lactam until cultures return, since both MRSA and streptococci must be covered.

questions.q: Cellulitis is around a small abscess that has just been drained in a patient with a history of MRSA. Which oral antibiotic fits?
questions.why: Purulence and a MRSA history each independently call for MRSA cover. Doxycycline is the usual alternative.

questions.q: Besides the antibiotic, what simple measure speeds recovery from leg cellulitis?
d: Applying ice for an hour at a time
questions.why: Oedema slows the clearing of infection and is itself a risk factor for the next episode, which is why compression comes in once the acute infection has settled.
